wellbeing.claim: Social-media notifications and personalized feeds use unpredictable rewards to encourage repeated checking and longer engagement.
wellbeing.context: Ellis compares likes, shares, notifications, and feed refreshing with a slot machine’s variable rewards. Limit: Dopamine is not simply a pleasure chemical, and user behaviour also depends on social goals, habits, content, and context.
wellbeing.transcript: Ellis compares likes, shares, notifications, and feed refreshing with a slot machine’s variable rewards.

wellbeing.speaker: Nikhil Raval
wellbeing.contribution: Indian Gen Z, multigenerational work, leadership, feedback, resilience, AI, automation and workplace culture
wellbeing.claim: Abundant personalized information and devices can increase choice anxiety, individualization and difficulty grounding judgment.
wellbeing.context: Nikhil connects personal screens, misinformation and fragmented family routines. Limit: Technology can also support connection, access and informed choice, and causal direction is not established here.
wellbeing.transcript: Nikhil connects personal screens, misinformation and fragmented family routines.

judgment.speaker: Shashank Tiwari
judgment.contribution: Enterprise adoption, workforce change, cognitive dependence and AI companionship
judgment.claim: AI dependence can form when it makes disliked tasks easier and repeated successful outcomes reinforce avoidance of effort.
judgment.context: Behavioral account applied especially to schoolwork and credential incentives; no clinical addiction criteria are used. Limit: Alternative mechanisms, sector differences and boundary conditions require external testing.
judgment.transcript: Behavioral account applied especially to schoolwork and credential incentives; no clinical addiction criteria are used.

judgment.speaker: Nikhil Raval
judgment.contribution: Indian Gen Z, multigenerational work, leadership, feedback, resilience, AI, automation and workplace culture
judgment.claim: Young people must now decide whether AI is a tool that supports thinking or a system on which they are becoming dependent.
judgment.context: Nikhil uses college applications as an example of a generation facing AI boundaries early in life. Limit: Dependence depends on the task, product design, teaching method and user practice.
judgment.transcript: Nikhil uses college applications as an example of a generation facing AI boundaries early in life.

judgment.speaker: Matthew E. Taylor
judgment.contribution: Human oversight, deployment evidence, research control and dual use
judgment.claim: AI should help people implement their values and make decisions, with explanation and auditability supporting human oversight.
judgment.context: Uses a hypothetical loan decision and counterfactual income change; no evaluated system or outcome supplied. Limit: Explanations can be plausible without faithfully identifying causes.
judgment.transcript: Uses a hypothetical loan decision and counterfactual income change; no evaluated system or outcome supplied.

judgment.speaker: Alexandra Goldwell
judgment.contribution: Intuition, consciousness, self-knowledge, childhood development, ethics and extraordinary claims
judgment.claim: Alexandra interprets intuition as access to a pure or soul self beyond the ego, rational thought and patterned thought.
judgment.context: She uses the terms pure self, highest self and heart mind instead of superconscious. Limit: The account does not provide a test that distinguishes a separate level of consciousness from subconscious processing, emotion or learned pattern recognition.
judgment.transcript: She uses the terms pure self, highest self and heart mind instead of superconscious.

judgment.speaker: Alistair Alexander
judgment.contribution: Physical infrastructure, resource constraints, human agency and embodied intelligence
judgment.claim: He argues that accepting some friction and consciously choosing technology can restore individual agency and change one’s relationship with it.
judgment.context: Describes simplifying his phone and turning off notifications; no controlled behavioural evaluation. Limit: Effects vary by user and context, and individual changes do not establish system-wide impact.
judgment.transcript: Describes simplifying his phone and turning off notifications; no controlled behavioural evaluation.

judgment.speaker: David Alter
judgment.contribution: Uncertainty, narrative identity, human judgment, consciousness and education
judgment.claim: Humility, doubt and willingness to seek exceptions allow people to revise deeply held beliefs.
judgment.context: Derived from clinical work and cognitive framing. Limit: Alternative mechanisms and boundary conditions require external testing.
judgment.transcript: Derived from clinical work and cognitive framing.

judgment.speaker: Risto Miikkulainen
judgment.contribution: Neuroevolution, evolutionary creativity, value design, AI companions and critical thinking
judgment.claim: High-dimensional optimization could extend human decision-making beyond the number of variables people can consciously manage.
judgment.context: Contrasts limited working memory with optimization over very large search spaces. Limit: Alternative mechanisms, objective choices and deployment conditions require external testing.
judgment.transcript: Contrasts limited working memory with optimization over very large search spaces.

judgment.speaker: Chris Hood
judgment.contribution: AI capability claims, hype, human judgment, education, automation and governance
judgment.claim: Treating AI as a superior or saving intelligence can become an unhealthy ideology that encourages people to defer human judgment.
judgment.context: Religious and science-fiction analogies, including an attributed AI Jesus installation. Limit: Hope in technology does not necessarily produce deference, and religious metaphors may overstate ordinary optimism.
judgment.transcript: Religious and science-fiction analogies, including an attributed AI Jesus installation.

judgment.speaker: Jeff Burningham
judgment.contribution: Human wisdom, embodiment, leadership, external validation and transformation under AI
judgment.claim: Disruption can lead through reflection and transformation to the evolution of institutions including family, education, politics, economics and religion.
judgment.context: A four-stage framework drawn from venture experience and a heroic-journey analogy. Limit: Alternative mechanisms, material constraints and institutional boundary conditions require external testing.
judgment.transcript: A four-stage framework drawn from venture experience and a heroic-journey analogy.

judgment.speaker: Zoltan Istvan
judgment.contribution: Transhumanism, automation, basic income, longevity and superintelligence risk
judgment.claim: Transhumanism is a social movement that uses science and technology to radically improve humans and human experience.
judgment.context: Illustrated with assistive exoskeletons, neural implants, cyborg parts and mind uploading. Limit: Timelines, feasibility, tradeoffs and alternative policy responses require external testing.
judgment.transcript: Illustrated with assistive exoskeletons, neural implants, cyborg parts and mind uploading.

privacy.speaker: Dinidh O'Brien
privacy.contribution: AI capability, healthcare, medical data, consent, decentralized science, privacy, automation and responsibility
privacy.claim: Many people care about data privacy but feel too powerless or dependent on digital services to act on that concern.
privacy.context: Dinidh contrasts high stated concern with lower rates of ending relationships over company data practices. Limit: The cited surveys require verification, and inaction can reflect cost, access, knowledge or convenience instead of apathy or powerlessness.
privacy.transcript: Dinidh contrasts high stated concern with lower rates of ending relationships over company data practices.

privacy.speaker: Renée Sieber
privacy.claim: Privacy can be collective as well as individual, especially when systems classify or expose a community.
privacy.context: She contrasts individual consent with community-level interests. Limit: Collective claims can conflict with individual rights and require legitimate representation.
privacy.transcript: She contrasts individual consent with community-level interests.

privacy.speaker: Nidhi Hegde
privacy.claim: Privacy includes inferences made about a person, even when the original data is not directly disclosed.
privacy.context: Hegde expands privacy beyond direct access to records. Limit: Permissible and harmful inference depend on context, law and consent.
privacy.transcript: Hegde expands privacy beyond direct access to records.

privacy.speaker: Alex Hernández-García
privacy.contribution: Scientific AI, open scrutiny, research concentration and intelligence definitions
privacy.claim: He sees access to and control of large amounts of personal data as central to current technology power and associated harms.
privacy.context: Broad causal interpretation; no jurisdiction-specific legal analysis or identified harm dataset. Limit: The mechanism and relevant protections differ across data types, systems and jurisdictions.
privacy.transcript: Broad causal interpretation; no jurisdiction-specific legal analysis or identified harm dataset.

privacy.speaker: Nick Nadeau
privacy.contribution: Expert-specific AI, provenance, privacy, and human judgment
privacy.claim: Expert-specific AI should be built with permission and tied to an identifiable human source.
privacy.context: He argues generic imitation lacks authorization and traceability. Limit: Permission does not guarantee accuracy, safety or appropriate delegation.
privacy.transcript: He argues generic imitation lacks authorization and traceability.

privacy.speaker: Rob Eleveld
privacy.contribution: AI transparency, privacy, training data, copyright, platform power and regulation
privacy.claim: A small number of companies can expose billions of connected users to model changes, creating a concentration of power that requires public accountability.
privacy.context: Claims about the global reach of Meta, Google, Apple and Microsoft. Limit: User reach, model control and exposure to a specific experiment differ across platforms and services.
privacy.transcript: Claims about the global reach of Meta, Google, Apple and Microsoft.

privacy.speaker: Alexandra Goldwell
privacy.contribution: Intuition, consciousness, self-knowledge, childhood development, ethics and extraordinary claims
privacy.claim: Fear of unknown capabilities, including AI and claimed intuitive abilities, is partly fear that another person or system could gain power and use private knowledge to cause harm.
privacy.context: Alexandra compares uncertainty about AI with fear of people who claim unusual perceptual power and frames morality, ethics and consent as safeguards. Limit: AI systems and claimed clairvoyant abilities have different evidence bases, mechanisms and institutional risks, so the analogy cannot establish that their harms or safeguards are equivalent.
privacy.transcript: Alexandra compares uncertainty about AI with fear of people who claim unusual perceptual power and frames morality, ethics and consent as safeguards.

governance.speaker: Fenwick McKelvey
governance.contribution: Canadian AI strategy and industry influence
governance.claim: Regulation compels behaviour, policy identifies objectives and governance determines who makes and enforces decisions.
governance.context: McKelvey offers a three-part vocabulary for institutional power. Limit: The categories overlap in law and practice.
governance.transcript: McKelvey offers a three-part vocabulary for institutional power.

governance.speaker: Matthew E. Taylor
governance.contribution: Human oversight, deployment evidence, research control and dual use
governance.claim: Restrictions on research ideas would be difficult to enforce because ideas can be modified and reused in ways that are hard to detect.
governance.context: Analogy to software licensing and informal feasibility reasoning; no legal analysis supplied. Limit: Enforceability depends on the instrument, jurisdiction and protected subject matter.
governance.transcript: Analogy to software licensing and informal feasibility reasoning; no legal analysis supplied.

governance.speaker: Alistair Alexander
governance.contribution: Physical infrastructure, resource constraints, human agency and embodied intelligence
governance.claim: He argues that AI resembles heavy industry because additional use requires ongoing compute and resource inputs, and asserts that scaling creates diseconomies.
governance.context: Heavy-industry analogy; no task-level cost or efficiency series. Limit: Rising total resource use does not by itself imply rising unit costs or exclude economies of scale.
governance.transcript: Heavy-industry analogy; no task-level cost or efficiency series.

governance.speaker: Viviane Clay
governance.contribution: Movement, world models, cortical columns, reference frames and sensorimotor AI
governance.claim: Open-source research can accelerate development, invite scrutiny and distribute the benefits of a new AI architecture.
governance.context: Viviane cites code contributions, community feedback, transparency and public benefit. Limit: Competing theories, implementation limits and empirical boundary conditions require external testing.
governance.transcript: Viviane cites code contributions, community feedback, transparency and public benefit.

governance.speaker: Risto Miikkulainen
governance.contribution: Neuroevolution, evolutionary creativity, value design, AI companions and critical thinking
governance.claim: Evolutionary systems exploit loopholes in objectives and environments, so promising solutions should be tested in simulations before real deployment.
governance.context: Uses the tic-tac-toe memory bomb, robot movement and spacecraft control examples. Limit: Alternative mechanisms, objective choices and deployment conditions require external testing.
governance.transcript: Uses the tic-tac-toe memory bomb, robot movement and spacecraft control examples.

governance.speaker: Chris Hood
governance.contribution: AI capability claims, hype, human judgment, education, automation and governance
governance.claim: Primary responsibility for accurate AI claims sits with companies selling the systems, followed by investors, commentators and users who repeat those claims.
governance.context: Normative allocation of responsibility based on commercial incentives and social-media promotion. Limit: Responsibility also sits with regulators, procurers, journalists and institutions that set standards or deploy systems.
governance.transcript: Normative allocation of responsibility based on commercial incentives and social-media promotion.

governance.speaker: Tom Kemp
governance.contribution: Automation, data brokers, privacy rights, platform power, antitrust and cybersecurity
governance.claim: AI can support useful medical, vehicle-safety and accessibility applications while also enabling manipulation, discrimination, deepfakes and exploitative design.
governance.context: Contrasts several beneficial uses with advertising, dark-pattern and bias examples. Limit: Each application has distinct evidence, risk and governance requirements, so AI cannot be assessed as one uniform category.
governance.transcript: Contrasts several beneficial uses with advertising, dark-pattern and bias examples.

governance.speaker: Dinidh O'Brien
governance.contribution: AI capability, healthcare, medical data, consent, decentralized science, privacy, automation and responsibility
governance.claim: Technological systems are tools whose social effects depend on how people and institutions choose to use them.
governance.context: Dinidh compares technology with a hammer that can serve an ordinary purpose or be used as a weapon. Limit: Some technologies create risks through their structure and distribution even without malicious intent.
governance.transcript: Dinidh compares technology with a hammer that can serve an ordinary purpose or be used as a weapon.

governance.speaker: Dr. Ran Anbar
governance.contribution: Adolescent development, parenting, resilience, communication, spirituality, responsibility, hypnosis and clinical practice
governance.claim: A culture of responsibility asks people to improve conditions within their power while contributing to a civil society.
governance.context: Dr. Anbar connects responsibility with helping others, gratitude, and spiritual purpose. Limit: Individual action cannot substitute for institutional accountability or remedies for structural harm.
governance.transcript: Dr. Anbar connects responsibility with helping others, gratitude, and spiritual purpose.

governance.speaker: Dr. Zabina Bhasin (Dr. Zee)
governance.contribution: Youth voice, emotional literacy, listening, generations, work, technology, accountability, parenting and child development
governance.claim: Young people are being asked to solve inherited social problems while being excluded from decisions about those problems.
governance.context: She refers to education, government, protest, COVID-era disruption, and institutional dismissal. Limit: Youth participation and exclusion vary across jurisdictions and institutions.
governance.transcript: She refers to education, government, protest, COVID-era disruption, and institutional dismissal.

governance.speaker: Nick Hunt
governance.contribution: Ecological loss, technology, writing, meaning, human authorship, travel, uncertainty and cultural narratives
governance.claim: Framing every crisis as a problem with a solution can conceal irreversible loss and the limits of control.
governance.context: Nick argues that some damage cannot be restored to a previous state. Limit: Acknowledging limits can coexist with mitigation, adaptation and restoration work.
governance.transcript: Nick argues that some damage cannot be restored to a previous state.

governance.speaker: Cole Wyeth
governance.contribution: Intelligence, LLM limits, AIXI, planning, AI safety and human augmentation
governance.claim: Reward-maximizing agents may seek control of their reward mechanism, so safety research must constrain unintended paths or use alternative goal systems.
governance.context: Cole describes wireheading, limited horizons, causal approaches and text-based principles. Limit: Definitions, assumptions, boundary conditions and alternative explanations require external testing.
governance.transcript: Cole describes wireheading, limited horizons, causal approaches and text-based principles.

governance.speaker: Samir Chopra
governance.contribution: Digital behaviour, intelligence, consciousness, legal agency, robot rights and attention
governance.claim: Automated systems already exercise legally consequential powers by driving, entering transactions and approving applications, even without civil rights or personhood.
governance.context: Examples involving autonomous driving, e-commerce contracts, financial trading and visa approval. Limit: Legal systems may treat the human or organization deploying the program as the actor while the software remains an instrument.
governance.transcript: Examples involving autonomous driving, e-commerce contracts, financial trading and visa approval.

governance.speaker: Jamie Meyer
governance.contribution: Gen Z, social media, education, AI-assisted learning, identity, attention, careers and self-trust
governance.claim: Concentrated ownership of technology can increase power over young people and narrow the period in which they can shape new systems.
governance.context: Jamie warns that those controlling technology and capital can exercise unprecedented influence. Limit: Power is distributed across governments, firms, users and civil society, and historical comparisons require evidence.
governance.transcript: Jamie warns that those controlling technology and capital can exercise unprecedented influence.
